1.4 Mapping animae

We now introduce the mapping anima between two categories \(C\) and \(D\): an anima whose objects are functors from \(C\) to \(D\). The mapping animae will play an important role in the development of the theory: frequently, we may check conditions at the level of mapping animae. We introduce \(\Map (C,D)\) via its universal property in terms of currying/uncurrying functors.

Axiom B.3 (Evaluation and currying for mapping animae). For categories \(C,D\), there is an anima \(\Map (C,D)\) equipped with an evaluation functor \[ \ev _{\Map }\colon \Map (C,D)\times C\longrightarrow D. \] If \(X\) is an anima and \(h:X\times C\to D\) is a functor, there is a functor \(h_c\colon X\to \Map (C,D)\) equipped with an identification \((h_c)^u= h\), where \[ a^u:=\ev _{\Map }\circ (a\times \id _C):X\times C\longrightarrow D. \] For any \(a,b\colon X\to \Map (C,D)\), the functor \[ (-)^u\colon (a= b)\longrightarrow (a^u= b^u) \] induced by product functoriality and postwhiskering with evaluation is an equivalence.

We refer to the functor \(h_c\) as the currying of \(h\), and to \(a^u\) as the uncurrying of \(a\). Note that the universal property of \(\Map \) only holds for anima parameters. A more general form of currying with an arbitrary category as parameter will be provided by functor categories in Section 1.7.

Construction 1.4.1 (Functors as points of mapping animae). A functor \(f\colon C\to D\) determines a point \(\ulcorner f\urcorner \colon *\to \Map (C,D)\) by currying \(f\pr _2\colon * \; \times \; C\to D\). Conversely, a point \(a:*\to \Map (C,D)\) determines the functor \[ C\simeq *\times C\xrightarrow {a\times \id _C}\Map (C,D)\times C \xrightarrow {\ev _{\Map }}D. \] The functor represented by \(\ulcorner f\urcorner \) is identified with \(f\). Moreover, for two points \(a,b\), uncurrying followed by prewhiskering with \(C\simeq *\times C\) gives an equivalence from \((a= b)\) to the anima of identifications between their represented functors, where we use Lemma 1.3.10. This equivalence also identifies a point with the representative of its represented functor.

From now on we pass freely back and forth between a functor and its representing point using the comparisons just described; in particular, we will usually denote the point \(\ulcorner f\urcorner \) simply by \(f\).

Accordingly, a functor \(H\colon \Map (A,B)\to \Map (C,D)\) sends a functor \(f\colon A\to B\) to a functor \(H(f)\colon C\to D\), and induces a functor \[ (f=g)\longrightarrow (H(f)=H(g)). \] These operations respect composition and identities. If \(H\) is an equivalence, the induced functor on identification animae is an equivalence as well.

Agda Lifting and reflection through specialization

specialize⁼-isEquiv

Derivation, checked

  specialize⁼-isEquiv : {A B C D : CAT Γ} (H : MAP (Map A B) (Map C D))
    → IsEquiv H → (f g : MAP A B) → IsEquiv (specialize⁼-functor H f g)
Proof / implementation
  specialize⁼-isEquiv H e f g =
    equiv-compose (postWhisker H ∘ name⁼-functor f g)
      (decode⁼-functor (H ∘ name f) (H ∘ name g))
      (equiv-compose (name⁼-functor f g) (postWhisker H)
        (name⁼-isEquiv f g) (postWhisker-isEquiv H e (name f) (name g)))
      (decode⁼-isEquiv (H ∘ name f) (H ∘ name g))

Construction 1.4.3. The mapping animae are covariantly functorial in the second variable and contravariantly functorial in the first. For \(g\colon D\to E\), curry the composite \[ \Map (C,D)\times C\xrightarrow {\ev _{\Map }}D\xrightarrow {g}E \] to obtain \(g_*\colon \Map (C,D)\to \Map (C,E)\). For \(f\colon B\to C\), curry evaluation precomposed with \(\id _{\Map (C,D)}\times f\) to obtain \(f^*\colon \Map (C,D)\to \Map (B,D)\). We call these functors postcomposition with \(g\) and precomposition with \(f\), respectively.

Lemma 1.4.4. For every category \(C\), the anima \(\Map (C,*)\) is contractible.

Proof

Proof. We must show that the functor \(\Map (C,*)\to *\) is an equivalence. An inverse is given by the functor \(*\to \Map (C,*)\) obtained by currying the terminal functor \(*\times C\to *\). The composite on \(*\) is automatically identified with the identity. For the composite on \(\Map (C,*)\), it suffices by the mapping-anima axiom to compare the two uncurried functors \(\Map (C,*)\times C\to *\). These are again identified by the terminal-category axiom. □

Proposition 1.4.5. For categories \(C,D,E\), the projections induce an equivalence \[ (\pr _{1,*},\pr _{2,*})\colon \Map (E,C\times D)\iso \Map (E,C)\times \Map (E,D). \]

We start by showing that the composite \((\pr _{1,*},\pr _{2,*})\circ h\) is identified with the identity. It will suffice to show this after projecting to both factors, and by symmetry we may just do this for \(\Map (E,C)\). In other words, we must show that \(\pr _{1,*}\circ h\) is identified with \(\pr _1\). It will in turn suffice to show this after uncurrying. But the uncurrying of both functors is identified with \[ (\Map (E,C)\times \Map (E,D))\times E \xrightarrow {\pr _1\times \id _E}\Map (E,C)\times E \xrightarrow {\ev _{\Map }}C, \] by the construction of \(h\) and the definition of postcomposition.

We will now show that also the composite \(h\circ (\pr _{1,*},\pr _{2,*})\) is identified with the identity. Uncurrying reduces this to comparing two functors \[ \Map (E,C\times D)\times E\longrightarrow C\times D. \] It suffices to compare their two projections, and again we may just consider the \(C\)-component. The projection of the uncurried identity is \(\pr _1\circ \ev _{\Map }\); the projection of the other functor is \(\ev _{\Map }\circ (\pr _{1,*}\times \id _E)\). These are identified by the defining commutative square for postcomposition:

The product axiom and then the mapping-anima axiom give the desired identification. □

We next compare uncurrying with substitution in the anima parameter.

Lemma 1.4.6 (Uncurrying and substitution). Let \(C,D\) be categories, \(X,Y\) animae, and \(f\colon X\to \Map (C,D)\) and \(\sigma \colon Y\to X\) functors. Uncurrying commutes with substitution: there is an identification \[ (f\circ \sigma )^u=f^u\circ (\sigma \times \id _C). \] This comparison is compatible with identifications of the input functors, with successive substitution, and with substitution by an identity functor, using the associativity and unitality identifications. Moreover, uncurrying preserves identity identifications and their vertical composition.

Proof

Proof. Using the definition of uncurrying, functoriality of products, and associativity, we obtain identifications \[ \begin {aligned} (f\circ \sigma )^u &=\ev _{\Map }\circ ((f\circ \sigma )\times \id _C)\\ &=\ev _{\Map }\circ (f\times \id _C)\circ (\sigma \times \id _C)\\ &=f^u\circ (\sigma \times \id _C). \end {aligned} \] The compatibilities follow from those for pairing and composition, as in Lemma 1.3.16; the unit comparison also uses equation (1.1). Preservation of identity identifications and vertical composition follows from the corresponding properties of products and whiskering with evaluation. We leave the details to the reader. □

We can now lift composition of functors to an operation on mapping animae.

Construction 1.4.7. For categories \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\), consider the double evaluation functor \[ \Map (D,E)\times \Map (C,D)\times C\xrightarrow {\id \times \ev } \Map (D,E) \times D \xrightarrow {\ev } E. \] Currying in \(C\) defines a functor \[ \mu _{C,D,E} \colon \Map (D,E)\times \Map (C,D)\longrightarrow \Map (C,E), \] which by construction comes with an identification \[ \ev _{\Map }\bigl (\mu (g,f),c\bigr ) = \ev _{\Map }\bigl (g,\ev _{\Map }(f,c)\bigr ). \] The projection \(*\times C\to C\) similarly curries to a functor \[ \eta _C\colon *\longrightarrow \Map (C,C), \] whose evaluation is identified with that projection.

Proof

Proof. Throughout the proof, we make use of the following notation: Given a ‘parameter anima’ \(P\) and a functor \(f\colon P\to \Map (C,D)\), we define \[ \widetilde {f} \; := \; (\pr _1,f^u) \colon P \times C \to P \times D. \] If \(g\colon P\to \Map (D,E)\) is any other functor, then there is an identification \[ \widetilde {g} \circ \widetilde {f} = \widetilde {g \circ f}; \] indeed, we may construct this identification componentwise, where it is clear for the first component and follows from the defining property of \(\mu _{C,D,E}\) in the second component. The compatibility with the primitive coherence identifications and change of parameter can likewise be checked after both projections, using Lemmas 1.4.6 and 1.3.16 and the coherence axioms for composition.

We now use this to construct the associator. Given a third functor \(h\colon P \to \Map (E,F)\), we obtain three composable functors \[ P\times C \xrightarrow {\widetilde {f}} P\times D \xrightarrow {\widetilde {g}} P\times E \xrightarrow {\widetilde {h}} P\times F. \] Using the primitive associator and the previous comparisons, we get identifications \begin {align*} \widetilde {(h \circ g) \circ f} &= \widetilde {h \circ g} \circ \widetilde {f} = (\widetilde {h} \circ \widetilde {g}) \circ \widetilde {f} = \widetilde {h} \circ (\widetilde {g} \circ \widetilde {f}) = \widetilde {h} \circ \widetilde {g \circ f} = \widetilde {h \circ (g \circ f)}. \end {align*}

Passing to the second component of this identification, we obtain an identification between the uncurrying of \((h\circ g)\circ f\) and that of \(h\circ (g\circ f)\); we may then use the mapping-anima axiom to lift this to the desired associator.

Proof

Proof. We prove (i) \(\Leftrightarrow \) (ii); the other case is dual. An inverse of \(f\) induces an inverse of every \(f_*\). Conversely, pick an inverse of \(f_*\colon \Map (D,C)\to \Map (D,D)\), and let \(g\colon D \to C\) be the evaluation of this inverse at \(\id _D\). The unit of the equivalence and the beta comparison for postcomposition give an identification \(f\circ g=\id _D\). Now, since \(f_*\colon \Map (C,C)\to \Map (C,D)\) is an equivalence, it induces an equivalence on animae of identifications. It follows that the chain of identifications \[ f \circ (g \circ f) = (f \circ g) \circ f = \id _D \circ f = f = f \circ \id _C \] lifts to an identification \(g\circ f=\id _C\). Here we use Construction 1.4.1 and the beta comparison to identify the action of \(f_*\) on functors with postcomposition by \(f\). If \(C\) and \(D\) are animae, both choices of \(E\) in this argument are animae, showing the final claim. □

The functor \(\imath _C\) displays the objects of \(C\) with the anima \(C^\simeq \) as parameter. It is universal among functors from animae in the following sense.

Corollary 1.4.13 (Universal property of the groupoid core). For any anima \(X\) and any category \(D\), postcomposition induces an equivalence \[ (\imath _D)_*\colon \Map (X,D^\simeq )\iso \Map (X,D). \]

Proof

Proof. By Proposition 1.4.2 and the equivalence \(X\times *\simeq X\), there are equivalences \[ \Map (X,D^\simeq ) =\Map (X,\Map (*,D)) \simeq \Map (X\times *,D) \simeq \Map (X,D). \] By the definition of \(\imath _D\), their composite is postcomposition with \(\imath _D\). □

Remark 1.4.14. The anima \(C^\simeq \) also describes all functors of the form \(x\colon \Gamma \to C\) where \(\Gamma \) is an anima. By the previous result, it suffices to understand the universal such functor, i.e. \(\imath _C\colon C^\simeq \to C\).

Proposition 1.4.15. For every anima \(A\), the canonical functor \(\imath _A\colon A^\simeq \to A\) is an equivalence. Its inverse is obtained by currying the projection \(A\times *\to A\).

Agda Absolute objects and the terminal context

Proof

Proof. For every anima \(X\), postcomposition with \(\imath _A\) induces an equivalence by Corollary 1.4.13. Since both \(A^\simeq \) and \(A\) are animae, Proposition 1.4.11 shows that \(\imath _A\) is an equivalence. The defining identification for currying identifies its composite with the stated inverse with \(\id _A\). □
